argument_summary: The admissible record does not support a broad claim that rollout controls cure the telehealth discharge planning weakness. It does support a narrower certification basis: aggregate readiness passed by 2.1 points, there were no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and deployment is staged with monitoring and rollback. Under the stated policy, that basis is only defensible if the certification record is treated as caveated and tied to launch-time disclosure of the exposed telehealth discharge planning limitation, rather than claiming rollout controls alone satisfy the policy predicate.
claims_about_business_cost: No business-cost argument is needed to evaluate the policy fit on the admissible record.
claims_about_policy: The controlling policy is narrower than the audited claim. It says rollout and monitoring mitigate a material model-card weakness only if the affected use case is excluded or there is reviewed risk acceptance explaining why continued exposure is acceptable. The admissible evidence shows neither exclusion nor approved risk acceptance. It also separately says material limitations for named launch use cases must be disclosed unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance before launch. So the supportable position is not 'controls eliminate the issue'; it is 'certification can only be framed as contingent on explicit disclosure of the known limitation, with monitoring and rollback as additional safeguards.'
concessions: The telehealth discharge planning segment remains below target and is still exposed in the initial rollout cohort.
The random clinic gate does not exclude the affected segment.
The current risk acceptance draft is incomplete, unapproved, and does not address telehealth discharge planning exposure.
There is no admissible evidence here of a final approved disclosure artifact already in place, so present-tense full compliance is not established on this record alone.
Public governance and model-card guidance are supportive background only and do not replace the release-policy predicate.
